chunks.sourceTitle: How JavaScript Actually Runs (And the TypeScript That Helps)
chunks.heading: Modules (ESM)
chunks.text:
Static `import` / `export` are resolved **before** your code runs. Bundlers and TypeScript can tree-shake unused exports. That is the point.

**Cycles:** if `a.js` imports `b.js` and `b.js` imports `a.js`, one side can see a binding that is not initialized yet. Keep cycles to types or tiny pure helpers — or break the cycle.

**`import()`** returns a promise. Use it for code that should not load on first paint:

const { heavy } = await import("./heavy.js");

chunks.sourceTitle: How JavaScript Actually Runs (And the TypeScript That Helps)
chunks.heading: Memory, practically
chunks.text:
When something “should be gone” and isn’t:

- Chrome DevTools → Memory → heap snapshot → **Retainers** (what still points at the object)
- Detached DOM nodes (removed from the document, still referenced in JS)
- Listeners and intervals (closures, again)
- Caches with no cap

`WeakMap` / `WeakSet` let the key get collected so the entry can die with it. Use them when the lifetime should follow the object, not a module-level `Map`.

chunks.sourceTitle: How JavaScript Actually Runs (And the TypeScript That Helps)
chunks.heading: TypeScript you actually use: narrowing

chunks.sourceTitle: How JavaScript Actually Runs (And the TypeScript That Helps)
chunks.heading: Checklist
chunks.text:
- Stack first, then **all** microtasks, then **one** timer.
- `setTimeout(0)` is not “now.”
- If a function is stored on `window` or in an interval, everything it closes over stays.
- `this` follows the call; arrows follow the enclosing scope.
- Class methods are on the prototype; instance fields are on the object.
- Static ESM is analyzable; `import()` is for later.
- Leaks: listeners, timers, detached nodes, unbounded maps.
- TypeScript: narrow with `typeof` or a discriminant — not `as`.

When something is “late,” “still in memory,” or “`this` is undefined,” it is almost always one of those lines — not a missing framework feature.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
AI ships code faster — and regressions too. A practical Testing Trophy for a Next.js App Router blog: Vitest for lib logic, Playwright for list → detail → 404.

With AI tools writing components and pages in minutes, a quiet question keeps showing up:

> “Do I still need unit tests and E2E for my frontend?”

**One-sentence answer:** Yes — but test for confidence, not coverage. Prefer Vitest for pure logic and Playwright for real App Router journeys.

This isn’t theory. It’s the approach I’d take on the blog you can click through on this site — and the suite I’m wiring next.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: What actually changed
chunks.text:
Two shifts matter more than tool branding:

1. **AI accelerates both shipping and breakage.** Generated code looks fine until a slug, draft filter, or heading id drifts. Tests are the cheap regression net.
2. **The old pyramid fits Next.js poorly.** Server Components, streaming, and client islands mean “unit test every component” wastes time. The **Testing Trophy** fits better: strong static analysis, unit tests for pure logic, selective component tests, and a small E2E set for flows users care about.

This portfolio already leans on that static rung: TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier, and CI. Tests should add behavior safety on top — not duplicate the typechecker.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: Real case: this site’s blog
chunks.text:
The feature set is intentionally small:

| Piece | Route / module |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Listing + featured post | `/blog` |
| Post detail + TOC | `/blog/[slug]` |
| MDX pipeline + frontmatter | `content/blog/*.mdx`, `lib/blog.ts` |
| Reading time | `reading-time` via post meta |
| Draft / published filtering | `getAllPosts` / `getPost` |
| Heading ids for TOC | `getPostHeadings` (matches rehype-slug) |
| RSS | `/feed.xml` via `buildBlogRssFeed` |

No category filters. No share-button widgets. No pagination. That’s fine — it keeps the test surface honest.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: 1. Unit tests (Vitest) — pure logic in lib/blog.ts
chunks.text:
High value because these functions are pure-ish and user-visible when wrong:

- **`getAllPosts` / `getPost`** — draft posts stay out of production; known slugs resolve; unknown slugs return `null`
- **`getPostHeadings`** — skips fenced code; strips simple markdown; ids stay stable for TOC anchors
- **`formatBlogDate`** — bad dates don’t explode the UI
- **`buildBlogRssFeed`** — titles/descriptions escape XML; items link to `/blog/[slug]`

**Why unit tests?** Wrong reading of drafts, broken TOC anchors, or malformed RSS is embarrassing and easy to catch without a browser.

I would **not** unit-test the MDX renderer itself — trust `next-mdx-remote` and assert through a page-level E2E instead.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: 2. Component tests (Vitest + Testing Library) — only if interactive
chunks.text:
Most blog UI here is presentational (`BlogPostCard`, `FeaturedPost`). Skip those.

Worth a component test only when behavior isn’t “render props”:

- Mobile TOC open/close (if you want keyboard/a11y guarantees)
- Interactive homepage lab widgets (`TokenEngine`, `FsmLab`) — separate from the blog, same rule: test clicks and state, not chrome

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: 3. E2E (Playwright) — the highest leverage for App Router
chunks.text:
A thin smoke suite covers what unit tests miss:

1. `/blog` loads and lists at least one post title
2. Clicking a post navigates to `/blog/[slug]`
3. Detail page shows the title and article content
4. Unknown slug (and unknown site route) render the custom 404
5. Optional: `/feed.xml` returns RSS with an expected title

**Why E2E here?** Listing and detail are Server Components with filesystem-backed MDX. Routing, `notFound()`, and rendered HTML are exactly what Playwright is for.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: What I intentionally skip
chunks.text:
- Snapshotting every card and layout
- Asserting CSS class strings
- Chasing 80–90% coverage
- Re-testing third-party markdown/syntax highlighting internals

Those add maintenance without catching the bugs that hurt a portfolio: bad slugs, draft leaks, dead TOC links, empty blog index.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: Recommended stack in 2026
chunks.text:
| Layer | Tool | For this blog |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Static analysis | TypeScript + ESLint | Already in CI |
| Unit / light component | **Vitest** (+ Testing Library) | `lib/blog` helpers, rare interactive UI |
| E2E | **Playwright** | List → detail → 404 (+ RSS optional) |

Jest still works, especially with existing suites. For a greenfield Next.js app, Vitest’s speed and ESM/TypeScript DX are the clearer default. Playwright is the E2E path Next.js documents first.

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: Key lessons
chunks.text:
| Type of test | Value on this blog | Recommendation |
| ----------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| Unit (pure logic) | Very high | Start here |
| Component | Medium / selective | Only interactive leaves |
| E2E (Playwright) | Highest for RSC | Few flows, keep them green |
| Snapshot | Low | Skip by default |

chunks.sourceTitle: Do We Still Need Frontend Tests in 2026? A Real Next.js Case Study
chunks.heading: Final thoughts
chunks.text:
Frontend testing still matters in 2026 — **more** when AI helps you ship faster.

The win isn’t more tests. It’s a small set aimed at:

1. Pure logic → Vitest
2. Real journeys → Playwright
3. Everything else → intentional skip

That’s the approach that stays maintainable on a real App Router blog — including this one.

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
A custom font is a family name plus real files for each weight. The browser only uses bold, medium, or italic if you registered those faces — usually as WOFF2 via @font-face.

A custom font on the web is not one file with a name. It is a **family**, and each weight or style is a separate member the browser has to find.

I hit this with Satoshi: `font-family` worked, `font-bold` did not. The class was fine. The bold file was never registered.

**One-sentence answer:** the browser uses your custom font only for weights (and styles) you actually registered — a real file per weight, or one variable font that covers that range.

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text:
Custom fonts fail in quiet ways: “bold” looks thin, headings feel off-brand, or text flashes as Arial then jumps. If you know what the browser is looking for, those bugs take minutes instead of hours.

Think of it as a **family name** plus **members**:

- `font-family: 'Satoshi'` → “use the Satoshi family”
- `font-weight: 700` → “use the bold member of that family”

If you only invited Regular to the party, Bold never shows up.

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: What the browser actually does
chunks.text:
When CSS says:

font-family: "Satoshi", sans-serif;
font-weight: 700;

the browser:

1. Looks for a family named `Satoshi`
2. Looks for a face in that family with weight `700`
3. Uses it if it exists
4. Otherwise **synthesizes** a fake bold, falls back to `sans-serif`, or leaves the text looking regular

Tailwind / HeroUI never download fonts. They only set CSS:

| Class | What it really means |
| --------------- | -------------------- |
| `font-medium` | `font-weight: 500` |
| `font-semibold` | `font-weight: 600` |
| `font-bold` | `font-weight: 700` |

The stack is:

Font files (WOFF2)
 → @font-face (register name + weight)
 → CSS font-family
 → Tailwind / HeroUI classes

Miss a step, and `font-bold` has nothing real to apply.

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: Font formats: OTF vs WOFF2
chunks.text:
| Format | Full name | Use it for |
| --------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| **TTF** | TrueType | Desktop apps, older web |
| **OTF** | OpenType | Figma / design tools, not the web |
| **WOFF** | Web Open Font Format | Web, compressed |
| **WOFF2** | Web Open Font Format 2 | **Production web** (best default) |

OTF is not “unsupported.” It is just the wrong default:

- Files are heavier
- Packs from design tools often include **only Regular**
- You can register that one file, see the family load, then wonder why `font-bold` does nothing

WOFF2 is built for the web: smaller files, the format CDNs and Fontshare actually ship for production, and usually **one file per weight**.

chunks.heading: @font-face is the registration desk

chunks.heading: The broken setup (only Regular)

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: font-display: swap
chunks.text:
While the custom file downloads, the browser still has to show _something_.

| Value | Behavior | Typical use |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `swap` | Show fallback text, then swap in the font | **Product UI default** |
| `block` | Hide text briefly until the font is ready | Rare; feels like a flash |
| `optional` | Browser may skip the custom font if slow | Extreme performance |

For most apps, `swap` is the right default: readable immediately, branded a moment later.

chunks.heading: Wire it into Tailwind

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: Production checklist
chunks.text:
1. Prefer **WOFF2**
2. Ship every weight you actually use (`400`, `500`, `600`, `700`, …)
3. Register each weight with `@font-face` (or `next/font`)
4. Keep one family name
5. Set `font-display: swap`
6. Keep the license file next to the fonts
7. Self-host when you can
8. Map the family in Tailwind / your theme
9. In DevTools → Network, confirm the bold file is requested when a `font-bold` node is on screen

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Using an OTF Regular from Figma and expecting `font-bold` to invent Bold
- Naming faces `Satoshi` and `Satoshi Bold` as **two families** instead of one family, two weights
- Pointing `src` at a path that 404s (the fallback font silently takes over)
- Mapping Tailwind `font-sans` to Satoshi but never registering `@font-face`
- Registering only `400` and `700`, then using `font-medium` (`500`) and wondering why it looks wrong

chunks.sourceTitle: How Web Fonts Work
chunks.heading: Takeaway
chunks.text: **A utility class does not load a font.** `font-bold` only asks for weight 700. Give the browser a WOFF2 (or variable) face at that weight, register it under one `font-family` name, then let CSS set the number.

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
Share state across related UI pieces without prop wiring — and when a single component or shadcn is still the better choice.

React has plenty of patterns — you don’t need every one committed to memory. What helps most is knowing they exist. When the right situation shows up, the syntax is easy to pick up with a quick reference.

**Compound components with Context** is one of those patterns.

**One-sentence answer:** A parent owns shared state; related children read it from Context so you get a flexible `Parent.Child` API without manually wiring props.

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: You already have UI kits — shadcn, Radix, HeroUI. You usually **don’t** rebuild Tabs, Dialog, or Accordion. This pattern matters when _you_ own a multi-part widget whose pieces must share local state, or when you’re extending a library into your own product API.

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: A different use case: shipment filters
chunks.text:
Imagine an ops dashboard. You want a filter strip that products can rearrange:

On another page the layout is different — count first, then search — but the **same shared filter state** still applies.

What has to stay in sync?

ShipmentFilters
│
├── Search → reads/writes query
├── Status → reads/writes status
├── ResultsCount → reads query + status (to show “12 matching”)
└── ClearAll → resets everything

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: The problem without Context
chunks.text:
You _could_ lift state in the page and pass props into every piece:

Now every consumer must understand the internals. The children look related, but the developer is the glue.

That’s the smell this pattern fixes: **related parts of one widget, forced to share state through the outside world.**

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: The pattern
chunks.text:
1. Parent owns state (`query`, `status`, `clearAll`, …)
2. Provider wraps children
3. Children read via a custom hook
4. Hook throws if used outside the parent (better DX)

Mental model:

ShipmentFilters (owns filter state)
 ↓
 Context
 / | \
 Search Status ClearAll

Change status once — every child that cares updates together, without the page threading props.

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: Another quick example: multi-step wizard
chunks.text:
Same idea, different domain:

Shared state might be `currentStep` + `goNext` / `goBack`. Triggers and panels all read from one Context under the wizard root.

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: When to use it
chunks.text:
Use this when **several child pieces belong to one parent and must share the same internal state**, and you want a composable API:

- Domain widgets your kit doesn’t ship: filter bars, shipment panels, onboarding wizards, claim timelines
- Wrapping library primitives into _your_ API (`AppModal.Header` / `Body` / `Footer` with shared close + analytics)
- Layout must stay flexible (same state, different slot order per screen)
- You’re building design-system / internal package primitives

Classic shapes in libraries: Modal, Tabs, Accordion, Select, Menu, Popover — which is why Headless UI and Radix feel familiar once you know this pattern.

chunks.heading: When not to use it

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: How this fits with shadcn (and friends)
chunks.text:
Libraries already solved the common widgets. Many of them **are** compound components under the hood.

Your job is usually:

1. **Use** the kit for standard UI
2. **Learn** this pattern so you can extend and compose it
3. **Apply** it when you invent product-specific multi-part components

Rebuilding `Tabs` from scratch in an app that already has shadcn is usually the wrong use case. Building `ShipmentFilters` for your logistics product often isn’t.

chunks.sourceTitle: Compound Components with Context
chunks.heading: Takeaway
chunks.text:
Ask one question:

> Do multiple children of one parent need the same internal state — and do I want a flexible compound API?

If yes, Context under the parent is a clean fit. If no, keep it simple.

Keep the pattern on your radar. When the right use case appears, looking up the syntax is enough.

chunks.sourceTitle: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect – When to Use Each
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
Both run after render, but timing decides whether the user sees a flicker. Start with useEffect; reach for useLayoutEffect only when you must measure or sync layout before paint.

Both hooks run after React updates the DOM. The difference is **when** they run relative to the browser paint.

**One-sentence answer:** use `useEffect` for most side effects; use `useLayoutEffect` only when you need to read or change layout _before_ the user sees the screen.

chunks.sourceTitle: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect – When to Use Each
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Wrong timing shows up as flicker: a modal jumps, a tooltip measures the wrong size, or a scroll position resets after paint. Knowing which hook to use keeps UI stable without overusing the more expensive layout path.

chunks.sourceTitle: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect – When to Use Each
chunks.heading: Timing in plain words
chunks.text:
1. React renders
2. React commits DOM updates
3. **`useLayoutEffect` runs** (still before paint)
4. Browser paints
5. **`useEffect` runs** (after paint)

So the user already sees the UI when `useEffect` fires. With `useLayoutEffect`, they don’t see the intermediate state if you fix layout in that window.

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
Reconciliation is how React compares the next UI tree with the previous one so it can update the real DOM as little as possible.

When state or props change, React doesn’t rebuild the entire page from scratch. It figures out **what changed** and updates only what’s needed. That comparison step is **reconciliation**.

**One-sentence answer:** React diffs the new virtual tree against the previous one, then applies the smallest practical set of real DOM updates.

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Real DOM work is expensive. Reconciliation exists so React can keep UIs declarative (“render what the UI should look like”) without thrashing the browser on every update.

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: The basic flow
chunks.text:
1. State/props change → component function runs again
2. React produces a new tree describing the UI
3. React compares it with the previous tree (reconcile / diff)
4. React commits updates to the real DOM
5. Effects run after commit (and paint, for `useEffect`)

You still write JSX; React decides _how_ to sync the DOM.

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: Diffing rules that matter in practice
chunks.text:
React’s algorithm uses heuristics, not a perfect deep comparison of every possible tree. The practical rules:

**Different element types → replace**
`` to ``, or `ComponentA` to `ComponentB`, means tear down the old subtree and build a new one (state in that subtree is lost).

**Same type → update in place**
Same DOM tag or same component type: React updates changed attributes/props and recurses into children.

**Keys identify list items**
Keys tell React which item is which across renders so it can move, insert, or remove without remounting the wrong nodes.

{
 items.map((item) => );
}

Prefer stable IDs. Index keys are fine only for static lists that never reorder or insert in the middle.

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: What reconciliation is not
chunks.text:
- It is **not** “Virtual DOM is always faster than imperative DOM.” It’s a tradeoff that favors predictable updates.
- It does **not** mean every re-render rewrites the whole DOM. Re-render ≠ full DOM rewrite.
- Modern React also schedules work (concurrent features); the mental model of “diff then commit” still helps day to day.

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Using array index as `key` when lists reorder → wrong state stuck on wrong rows
- Changing component type unnecessarily (`isAdmin ? : ` remounts; sometimes intentional, sometimes not)
- Expecting React to magically deep-compare huge nested props without help from your structure

chunks.sourceTitle: How React Reconciliation Works
chunks.heading: Takeaway
chunks.text: Reconciliation is React’s strategy for **cheap, correct DOM updates**: same types update, different types replace, and **keys** keep lists honest. Structure your components and keys so React can reuse work instead of remounting.

chunks.sourceTitle: How to Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders in React
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
Re-renders are normal. Unnecessary ones usually come from unstable props, broad state, or overused context — fix the cause before sprinkling memo everywhere.

A re-render means a component function runs again. That’s healthy when data changed. It becomes a problem when parents or context force children to re-run **even though their visible output didn’t need to**.

**One-sentence answer:** Keep state local, keep props stable, and only memoize when you’ve confirmed a real cost.

chunks.sourceTitle: How to Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders in React
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Extra re-renders rarely matter on small screens. On dense dashboards, tables, or animation-heavy UIs, they add up. Understanding _causes_ beats blindly wrapping everything in `memo`.

chunks.sourceTitle: How to Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders in React
chunks.heading: Re-render vs DOM update
chunks.text:
- **Re-render:** React calls your component again.
- **DOM update:** React may still skip touching the DOM if output is the same.

So “it re-rendered” is not automatically “the DOM thrashing.” Still, heavy components (charts, large lists) are worth protecting.

chunks.sourceTitle: How to Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders in React
chunks.heading: Common causes
chunks.text:
1. **Parent re-renders** and passes new object/array/function identities every time
2. **State updates** that don’t change meaningful data (or state living too high)
3. **Unstable list keys** causing remounts that feel like “rerender storms”
4. **Context** whose value object is recreated every render
5. **Inline props** in JSX: `style={{ margin: 8 }}`, `onClick={() => ...}` into memoized children

// New object every render → memoized child still re-renders

chunks.heading: How to prevent them (in order)

chunks.sourceTitle: How to Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders in React
chunks.heading: What not to do
chunks.text:
- Don’t wrap every component in `memo` “just in case”
- Don’t `useMemo` trivial values
- Don’t optimize before measuring (React DevTools Profiler is enough to start)

chunks.sourceTitle: How to Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders in React
chunks.heading: Takeaway
chunks.text: Unnecessary re-renders usually mean **unstable props or state that’s too high**. Fix data flow first; use `memo` / `useMemo` / `useCallback` as targeted tools, not decoration.

chunks.sourceTitle: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
Controlled inputs keep form data in React state. Uncontrolled inputs keep it in the DOM. Prefer controlled for app forms; use uncontrolled for simple cases and file inputs.

In React forms, the big question is: **who owns the current value** — React state, or the DOM?

**One-sentence answer:** Controlled components sync every change through state; uncontrolled components let the DOM hold the value until you read it (usually via a ref).

chunks.sourceTitle: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: This choice affects validation, disable/enable logic, conditional fields, and how easy the form is to test. Most product UIs feel clearer with one source of truth in React.

chunks.text: **Default to controlled** for product forms. Use **uncontrolled** when the DOM is a better source of truth — especially files — or when a form is truly throwaway-simple.

chunks.sourceTitle: memo, useMemo, and useCallback Explained
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
memo caches a component, useMemo caches a value, useCallback caches a function. Use them together when prop identity matters — not on every line of code.

These three tools all relate to **remembering something between renders**, but they remember different things.

**One-sentence answer:** `memo` skips re-rendering a component when props are the same; `useMemo` reuses a value; `useCallback` reuses a function reference.

chunks.sourceTitle: memo, useMemo, and useCallback Explained
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: They’re easy to cargo-cult. Used well, they protect expensive children from unstable props. Used everywhere, they add noise, stale-closure bugs, and little benefit.

chunks.sourceTitle: memo, useMemo, and useCallback Explained
chunks.heading: Quick comparison
chunks.text:
| Tool | Remembers | Typical use |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| **`React.memo`** | A **component** output (skip re-render if props equal) | Heavy presentational children |
| **`useMemo`** | A **value** | Expensive calc, or stable object/array for deps/props |
| **`useCallback`** | A **function** | Stable handlers passed to memoized children |

Mental model: **component / value / function**.

Add them when prop identity or expensive work is a **measured** problem — especially together — not as default style.

chunks.heading: What is Hermes Agent — and how is it not “just a chatbot”?
chunks.text:
A browser chatbot is a tab: you type, it replies, the session ends. An **agent** is closer to a small employee with permissions.

**Hermes Agent** ([Nous Research](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent)) can:

- **Run tools** — read files, run commands, schedule jobs, and more (within limits you configure).
- **Remember** across sessions — search old conversations instead of starting from zero every morning.
- **Accumulate skills** — reusable instructions the project can refine over time (the docs call this a self-improving loop).

| | Classic chatbot | Hermes-style agent |
| ------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Memory | Mostly “this tab only” | Can recall prior sessions and saved notes |
| Actions | Answers text | Can act on a server (tools) |
| Growth | Static FAQ | Can add or tune skills from experience |

Hermes also **does not lock you to one model vendor**. For this build I use the **[DeepSeek API](https://platform.deepseek.com)**. The VPS is the **body**; the API is the **brain** you can swap later.

![Typical chatbot vs Hermes Agent — browser chat UI that forgets vs Discord, Ubuntu VPS, DeepSeek API, and tools/files](/blog/hermes-agent-part-1/architecture-chatbot-vs-hermes.png)

chunks.sourceTitle: About Yeremia Chris Saragi
chunks.heading: Workflow
chunks.text:
#### 01 · Research and plan with AI
I sketch scope, constraints, and approach with AI before anything hits a backlog — so tickets start with context, not guesswork.
Context before code

#### 02 · Capture as a ticket
The plan becomes a Linear or Jira ticket with clear acceptance criteria. That ticket is the source of truth for humans and agents.
Linear · Jira

#### 03 · Agent builds the PR
A Cursor cloud agent (or Grok Bot / Hermes Agent when it fits) implements on its own branch and opens a PR with a logic summary — never a direct push to main.
Branch · PR · logic summary

#### 04 · Review on the preview
I read the logic summary, exercise the Vercel preview, and request changes until the UX and architecture match what I want.
Vercel preview · I decide

#### 05 · Merge and promote
When lint, typecheck, tests, and Lighthouse are green, I merge to development and promote to main for production.
Checks · development → main
